item.title: Apple Unveils the iPhone Duo, a Foldable Phone That Costs $1,999
item.description: At the company’s annual September product event, Apple also demonstrated its work on artificial intelligence and other new devices.
item.dc:creator: Kalley Huang
item.media:credit: Jason Henry for The New York Times
item.media:description: Apple chief executive John Ternus introduced Duo, a foldable iPhone, on Wednesday.

item.title: How Amazon’s Zoox Is Taking On Waymo in San Francisco
item.description: The Amazon-owned driverless car company is a distant second to Waymo. Its pitch to riders? Wine pop-ups, festival sponsorships and a car built to be filmed.
item.dc:creator: Emmy Martin
item.media:credit: Kelsey McClellan for The New York Times
item.media:description: Zoox, owned by Amazon, offers free rides in San Francisco, which has become a center for autonomous vehicle experiments.

item.title: OpenAI Says It Has Cracked One of Math’s ‘Millennium Problems’
item.description: The company’s announcement is the most dramatic sign yet that artificial intelligence is fundamentally transforming the field of higher mathematics.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz
item.media:credit: Philippe Plailly/Science Source
item.media:description: Related to a set of equations about fluid mechanics, the “Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem” has long ranked among the great unsolved problems in mathematics.

item.title: The Mic Is On. So Is Live Auto-Tune.
item.description: As audiences demand perfection from live performances, pitch correction technology has become an increasingly common way for singers to deliver.
item.dc:creator: Malia Mendez
item.media:credit: Joseph Okpakko/WireImage, via Getty Images
item.media:description: The girl group Flo performing in London last year. The Grammy-nominated trio typically use some level of live Auto-Tune to smooth out their vocals, they said.

item.title: Elon Musk Has Pledged to Rid His Platform, X, of Child Sexual Abuse, but It Persists
item.description: Reviews by the Canadian Center for Child Protection and The New York Times found that explicit images of children remain on the social media site owned by Elon Musk.
item.dc:creator: Kate Conger and Michael H. Keller
item.category: National Center for Missing and Exploited Children
item.media:credit: Andres Kudacki for The New York Times
item.media:description: Elon Musk bought X, which was then known as Twitter, in 2022 and vowed to remove child sexual abuse material from the site, calling it “Priority #1.”

item.title: The Ezra Klein Show: The A.I. Revolt Is Here
item.description: The A.I. giants weren’t prepared for this.
item.dc:creator: Ezra Klein and Rollin Hu
item.media:credit: The New York Times

item.title: Could A.I. Really Kill All Humans?
item.description: After an Anthropic researcher quit, warning that the A.I. race is “gambling with our lives,” Cade Metz joined Natalie Kitroeff on “The Call” to break down what’s at stake.

item.title: California’s Governor Signs Landmark Online Child Safety Bills
item.description: Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a bill that prohibits social media platforms from providing addictive features to users under 16, the first law of its kind in the nation.
item.dc:creator: Cecilia Kang and Laurel Rosenhall
item.media:credit: Eric Ryan Anderson for The New York Times
item.media:description: Gov. Gavin Newsom’s actions follow a series of social media trials this year, in which thousands of teenagers, schools and states have accused Meta, Snap, TikTok and YouTube of hooking young users with products being compared to cigarettes.

item.title: Anthropic Says It Blocked Possible Efforts to Build Biological Weapons
item.description: In a new report, the A.I. start-up added that it could not determine whether the research was legitimate or nefarious, leading the company to shut down the work.
item.dc:creator: Dustin Volz
item.media:credit: Marissa Leshnov for The New York Times
item.media:description: The report Anthropic published on Thursday cataloged a litany of misuses of its A.I. models, including the chatbot Claude, over the past eight months.

item.title: How the New iPhone Duo’s Glass Screen Bends Without Breaking
item.description: The screens of foldable phones are a triumph of materials science and microengineering.
item.dc:creator: William J. Broad
item.media:credit: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg, via Getty Images

item.title: Why is Apple’s New Foldable iPhone Duo $1,999?
item.description: The company unveiled a new iPhone that costs $1,999. Here are the economics behind that price tag.
item.dc:creator: Brian X. Chen
item.media:credit: Jason Henry for The New York Times
item.media:description: Apple’s iPhone Duo will cost $1,999 when it arrives in October to compete with Samsung’s $1,900 Galaxy foldable.

item.title: Anthropic Researchers Raise Alarm Over A.I. Acceleration, Warning of Threat to Humanity
item.description: Their warnings echo concerns that other artificial intelligence experts have voiced in recent months, as calls increase for a slowdown in the pace of development.
item.dc:creator: Kate Conger
item.media:credit: Lucas Foglia for The New York Times
item.media:description: A protest outside Anthropic’s offices in San Francisco.

item.title: Why California Is Reconsidering Its Decision to Shun Nuclear Power
item.description: The state is considering extending the life of its last nuclear power plant, Diablo Canyon, and allowing construction of new reactors to help meet its clean energy goals.
item.dc:creator: Ivan Penn and Adam Perez
item.media:description: Established nuclear plants like Diablo Canyon in California tend to produce relatively affordable power.

item.title: Meta Introduces Muse, an A.I. Agent That Can Send Your Emails and Book Your Travel
item.description: Muse, Meta’s new A.I. agent, acts as a personal digital assistant that connects to Facebook and Instagram, as well as third-party apps such as Spotify and OpenTable.
item.dc:creator: Eli Tan

item.title: Apple Expected to Unveil a Folding iPhone at Annual Launch Event
item.description: Fans of the company’s products widely believe it will unveil a folding smartphone at its annual launch event on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Kalley Huang
item.media:credit: Lexi Parra/The New York Times
item.media:description: The look of Apple’s iPhones hasn’t changed that much over the years.

item.title: A Hacking Tool Built With A.I. Can Breach Phones Without a Click
item.description: An attack discovered by A.I. researchers could have compromised hundreds of millions of devices within hours, experts said.
item.dc:creator: Dustin Volz
item.media:credit: Dado Ruvic/Reuters
item.media:description: Researchers at Calif, a security company, recently built a hacking tool in a little more than a week that could run roughshod across WeChat, the popular messaging platform.

item.title: Key App Developers Have Yet to Embrace Apple’s New Siri A.I.
item.description: For the company’s new artificial intelligence system to take off, it will need plenty of support from the makers of popular apps on Apple’s phones.
item.dc:creator: Kalley Huang and Brian X. Chen
item.media:credit: Jason Henry for The New York Times
item.media:description: The new Siri is a revamp of Apple’s A.I. technology.

item.title: Virtual Taekwondo Takes the Contact Out of a Combat Sport
item.description: The contactless version of the Korean martial art is making its debut at this year’s Asian Games. Critics say it’s a glorified video game.
item.dc:creator: Yan Zhuang and Jean Chung

item.title: Early Data Indicates an A.I.-Generated Drug Could Slow Aging
item.description: Artificial intelligence was used to help develop a drug candidate, rentosertib, for a rare lung condition. Its maker says the drug also seems to reduce the biological hallmarks of age.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz
item.media:credit: Laurie Chen/Reuters
item.media:description: Rentosertib, Insilico Medicine’s small-molecule drug candidate developed and designed using generative A.I. for treating chronic lung disease, at the company’s research and development facility in Shanghai.

item.title: How a Blacklisted Chinese Tech Giant Kept Buying America’s Best A.I. Chips
item.description: Washington imposed sanctions on Inspur because of its work with the Chinese military. But the company’s subsidiary kept shipping Nvidia’s best chips to feed China’s leading A.I. firms.
item.dc:creator: Ana Swanson, Paul Mozur, Tripp Mickle and Keith Bradsher
item.media:credit: Minh Connors for The New York Times
item.media:description: Aivres’s research and development technology center and manufacturing facility in Fremont, Calif.

item.title: Authors Wrangle With Publishers Over $1.5 Billion Anthropic A.I. Settlement
item.description: The tech giant must pay $3,000 per pirated book that it used to train its chatbot. Many authors fear they could lose funds to others in the book business.
item.dc:creator: Neil Vigdor
item.media:credit: Jason Henry for The New York Times
item.media:description: An Anthropic logo at an event in San Francisco in May. The tech giant will have to pay more than $1.5 billion in a settlement over using books to train its chatbots.

item.title: Kenyans Made a Living Writing College Essays. Then A.I. Arrived.
item.description: Thousands of Kenyans made a living writing essays for overseas students. With A.I., the work has dried up, a warning for online gig work that has been a global lifeline.
item.dc:creator: Adam Satariano and Paul Mozur
item.media:credit: Kang-Chun Cheng for The New York Times
item.media:description: Teresios Bundi, who ran an essay-writing business catering to overseas students, said his experience with artificial intelligence was a warning for online gig workers.

item.title: The Generation That’s Never Had to Say ‘Hello?’
item.description: Now that there’s rarely any mystery to who’s calling, Gen Z has adopted a range of custom phone greetings — including no greeting at all.
item.dc:creator: Alisha Haridasani Gupta

item.title: Court Filings In A.I. Suit Invoke Copyright Law, Culture and Sports
item.description: Filings made Friday in The New York Times’s closely watched lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft included a range of copyright law and cultural references.
item.dc:creator: Mike Isaac and Karen Weise
item.media:credit: Zack DeZon for The New York Times
item.media:description: The New York Times claims in a lawsuit that OpenAI and Microsoft infringed on publishers’ copyrighted material by using their articles to train artificial intelligence.

item.title: F.B.I. Investigates Sale of Millions of Stolen Driver’s Licenses
item.description: The blog Krebs on Security reported on an identity theft service trying to sell scans of licenses and other documents belonging to people in Canada and the United States.
item.dc:creator: Christine Hauser
item.media:credit: Tierney L. Cross/The New York Times
item.media:description: The F.B.I. is looking into the sale of stolen scanned identity documents.

item.title: Tumbler Ridge Shooting Survivors File 30 Lawsuits Against OpenAI
item.description: The survivors contend that the company should have notified the police when it shut down the shooter’s disturbing ChatGPT account eight months before the February attack in British Columbia.
item.dc:creator: Michael Levenson
item.media:credit: Paige Taylor White/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: A memorial for the victims of a deadly mass shooting at a school in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, in February.

item.title: Corporate America Is Getting Hooked on Open-Source A.I.
item.description: Companies like AT&T are increasingly using cheap, freely available artificial intelligence models over expensive ones from Anthropic and OpenAI.
item.dc:creator: Eli Tan
item.media:credit: Josie Norton

item.title: Tesla’s Cybercab Is Being Investigated by Federal Regulators
item.description: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said it would examine whether the company’s new self-driving taxi, which has no steering wheel, meets federal auto regulations.
item.dc:creator: Jack Ewing
item.media:credit: Kaylee Greenlee/Reuters
item.media:description: A Tesla Cybercab in Austin, Texas, where the company has started offering paid rides in the driverless vehicles.
